chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text:
Nick Doty said:

like, the chair assesses whether the response to the objections is a strong technical decision, which kinda sounds like what the chair's opinion is

I am saying I don't agree with that. The notion of whether there is consensus is independent of whether it's a good idea. For example, the ADs are expected to independently assess document readiness

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text: I don't agree that the chair's technical assessment of the quality of people's technical positions is a relevant factor in the determination of consensus. Suppose that we have 40 people making argument A and 40 people making argument B, the chairs should not say "Argument A is without merit and therefore we have consensus"

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: ekr, okay yes, agreed, that was the concern I was trying to express as well. sorry for the confusion/double negatives.

chat.author: Joel Halpern
chat.text: I like one of the points in 7282 thata even an isolated technical issue must be addressed (not necesssarily agreed to, but addressed).  As far as I can tell, the chairs in the end have to judge whether such objections were competently addressed.  So they end up making technical judgements.

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: @joel, substantively addressed? or responded by a stronger technical argument?

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text:
Joel Halpern said:

I like one of the points in 7282 thata even an isolated technical issue must be addressed (not necesssarily agreed to, but addressed).  As far as I can tell, the chairs in the end have to judge whether such objections were competently addressed.  So they end up making technical judgements.

I actually don't agree with this. Rather, I think that assessment is made by determining whether the WG has rough consensus about whether the objection has been addressed

chat.author: Joel Halpern
chat.text: I have seen situations wher ethe WG was convinced something was right, and someone pointed out a technically valid issue.  The WG started wanting to dismiss the issue.  The chair (in my view correctly) forced the working group to actually engage.   In the case I can remember, the WG made changes to address the issue.  But that is not necessarily the result.  The WG can actually technically analyze the objection and decide it is wrong.

chat.author: Sean Turner
chat.text: Are we overcorrecting here?

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text:
Eric Rescorla said:

Joel Halpern said:

I like one of the points in 7282 thata even an isolated technical issue must be addressed (not necesssarily agreed to, but addressed).  As far as I can tell, the chairs in the end have to judge whether such objections were competently addressed.  So they end up making technical judgements.

I actually don't agree with this. Rather, I think that assessment is made by determining whether the WG has rough consensus about whether the objection has been addressed

As I said, I think occasionally the chair may feel that a given objection is fatal and that is part of their responsibility to refuse to advance a document in that case, but that's distinct from "here was an argument for doing A not B and I don't agree with the rebuttal to A but the rest of the WG did"
